sections.b: The first account is built with care. Ten times "God said"; seven times "it was good." Days one to three separate (light from dark, waters above from below, sea from land); days four to six fill what was separated (lights, birds and fish, land animals and humans). The seventh day crowns the week. God names things on the first three days, blesses on the fifth, sixth and seventh, and creates (bara) at the three high points: heaven and earth, the first living creatures, and humans.

The second account narrows from the cosmos to one garden and one couple. God is called "the LORD God" and works like a potter, a gardener and a builder. The order of telling is different (man, garden, animals, woman), which source critics take as a sign of a second source and traditional readers as a close-up of the sixth day (see the note at 2:4).

common: Genesis 1 says God made the world from nothing in so many words.
uncommon: Genesis 1 never calls the sun and moon by name, perhaps to avoid the names of gods.

claude.title: Three "not yet"s and three answers
claude.body: My own observation, which overlaps with Kline's reading of 2:5: Genesis 2:5–6 names three things missing before the garden: no rain, no one to work the ground, and (implied) no plants. The chapter answers each in reverse: God plants (2:8–9), sets a man to work the soil (2:15), and the river waters it (2:10). The story moves from lack to provision, as chapter 1 moves from emptiness to fullness.

sections.h: What the text of Genesis 1 offers each view
sections.b: Each view leans on real features of the text. For ordinary days: the numbered days, "evening and morning," and Exodus 20:11. For long days: yom means a whole period in 2:4 ("on the day the LORD God made"), the sixth day is full of events (2:7–23), and the seventh has no evening. For a framework: light appears on day one but the lights on day four, and the two triads mirror each other. For a temple reading: the seven-day pattern of temple building and dedication (1 Kings 8:65–66) and God's "rest" as enthronement. The days are numbered without "the" until the sixth, a detail every side explains differently.
sections.refs: Genesis 1:5; Genesis 1:14–19; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:2–4; Exodus 20:11; 1 Kings 8:65–66

claude.title: The days as a liturgy
claude.body: My own suggestion, close to Walton and to older Jewish readings of the creation week as a liturgy: the repeated lines ("God said... and so it was... God saw that it was good... evening came, and morning came") read like a responsive chant, built to be recited. If the account was shaped for worship, its exact structure would serve memory and praise, which could explain both its careful numbering and its lack of interest in mechanism. This does not decide the length of the days; it suggests why the question of length is not the text's own concern.

sections.b: Humankind is made "in our image, as our likeness" and at once told to rule (1:26–28). Adam then fathers Seth "in his likeness, by his image" (5:3), showing that the image is handed down after the fall. After the flood the image is the reason murder must be punished (9:6). The plural "let us" and the shift from "him" to "them" in 1:27 have been read many ways (see the notes at 1:26).

The creation week ends with a day God blesses and sets apart as holy (2:3), the first thing in the Bible called holy. It has no "evening and morning." The word Sabbath does not appear until Exodus 16, but the verb shavat does (2:2–3), and the Ten Commandments cite this passage (Exodus 20:11). Sevens also mark the flood story (7:4, 10; 8:10, 12).

Genesis 2:2–3 uses shavat, "stop," for God's rest. The other rest word, nuach, sounds through the flood story: Noah's name (5:29), the ark coming to rest (8:4), the dove finding no resting place (8:9), and the "soothing" smell of the sacrifice (8:21).

sections.h: The man and the woman in Genesis 2–5
sections.b: Genesis calls the first man ha-adam, "the human," and he becomes "Adam" as a name only gradually (2:20; 3:17, 21; 4:25; 5:1). He is shaped from the ground (adamah), set in the garden to work and guard it, and given the one command. The woman is built from his side as "a helper who is his match" (2:18); he names her Woman and, after the curse, Eve, "mother of everyone living" (3:20). Their sons are Cain, Abel and Seth, and Adam fathers other sons and daughters and dies at 930 (5:4–5).
sections.refs: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:18–23; Genesis 3:20; Genesis 4:1–2; Genesis 4:25; Genesis 5:1–5

common: Eve was made from Adam's rib, so men have one fewer rib.
The forbidden fruit was an apple.
uncommon: Some rabbis read the first human as created double, male and female, and then separated (Genesis Rabbah 8:1).

sections.b: Eden lies in the east; four rivers branch from it, two of them the Tigris and Euphrates. The garden has every good tree, the tree of life, and the tree of knowing good and evil. Gold, onyx, cherubim at an eastern gate, and God "walking about" (3:8) have led many to read it as the first sanctuary (see the notes at 2:13 and 2:15). After the sin the humans are sent out east, and cherubim guard the way back (3:23–24). Cain goes further east, to Nod (4:16).

Many scholars read Genesis 1–3 with temple eyes. Gordon Wenham pointed out that the garden has features of the tabernacle and temple: God walks there (3:8; Leviticus 26:12), the man is set to "work and guard" it like a Levite (2:15; Numbers 3:7–8), gold and onyx are found there (2:12; Exodus 28:9–12), the entrance is on the east and guarded by cherubim (3:24; Exodus 26:31), and a river flows from it (2:10; Ezekiel 47:1–12). John Walton reads Genesis 1 itself as the inauguration of the cosmos as God's temple, with the seventh day as his enthronement. The Bible ends with a city that is all temple and garden (Revelation 21:22; 22:1–2).
sections.refs: Genesis 2:10–15; Genesis 3:8; Genesis 3:24; Leviticus 26:12; Numbers 3:7–8; Exodus 26:31; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Revelation 21:22; Revelation 22:1–2

sections.b: The tree of life stands "in the middle of the garden" (2:9). It is never forbidden; after the sin God bars the way to it so that the man will not "live forever" in that state (3:22–24), and cherubim guard it. Gilgamesh's lost plant of youth, stolen by a snake, is a partial parallel. Revelation reopens the way (Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14).
sections.refs: Genesis 2:9; Genesis 3:22–24; Proverbs 3:18; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2; Revelation 22:14

sections.b: The snake questions God's word (3:1) and denies the penalty (3:4). The woman sees, desires, takes and eats, and gives to the man, who is with her (3:6). Their eyes open to shame (3:7). They hide; God calls; blame passes from man to woman to snake (3:8–13). God curses the snake and the ground and announces pain in childbirth, struggle in marriage, hard labor and death (3:14–19), but also clothes them (3:21) and promises that the woman's offspring will strike the snake (3:15). The word "sin" first appears with Cain (4:7), and the evil of the human heart is diagnosed in 6:5 and 8:21.

common: Eve ate while Adam was away.
uncommon: In Jewish tradition the episode shows the birth of the evil inclination rather than inherited guilt.

sections.b: The "ancient serpent" of Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 points back to the snake of Genesis 3, "shrewder than every wild animal" (3:1). Genesis itself never calls the snake the devil; it is a creature that speaks, deceives and is cursed to crawl and eat dust (3:14). The identification grew in Jewish writings (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) and the New Testament (John 8:44; Romans 16:20; 2 Corinthians 11:3). Genesis 3:15 promises the snake's head will be struck. The sea monsters (tanninim) of 1:21, the dragon-like creatures of Hebrew poetry, are simply part of God's creation in Genesis 1.
sections.refs: Genesis 3:1–15; Genesis 1:21; John 8:44; Romans 16:20; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2

sections.h: From the woman's offspring to Abram
sections.b: In Genesis 1–11 the word zera, "offspring," moves from plants that make seed (1:11–12, 29) to the woman's offspring (3:15), to Seth as "another offspring" (4:25), to Noah's offspring with whom God makes covenant (9:9). The genealogies of chapters 5 and 11 trace that line to Abram, and the section closes with Sarai's barrenness (11:30), so that the next promise of offspring (12:7) will depend wholly on God.

claude.title: Two lines of offspring
claude.body: My own reading, which builds on a common observation: 3:15 speaks of two "offsprings," the snake's and the woman's. Genesis 4–11 can be read as tracing both: Cain's line, with violence and a song of revenge (4:17–24), and Seth's, with worship and Enoch's walk with God (4:26; 5:22–24). Augustine's "two cities" is a version of the same idea. The text does not label Cain's line as the snake's, though 1 John 3:12 calls Cain "of the evil one."

sections.b: The chapter is built around the word "brother," used seven times in 4:2–11. God warns Cain in words that echo 3:16 ("its desire is for you, but you must rule over it," 4:7). Cain's words to Abel are missing from the Hebrew (see the variant at 4:8). The punishment drives Cain from the soil, and the sign protects him (4:15). His family builds the first city and founds herding, music and metalwork, ending with Lamech's boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge (4:17–24), which Jesus reverses (Matthew 18:22).

common: The mark of Cain was dark skin.
uncommon: Cain's name may mean "smith," which fits his family of metalworkers.

sections.b: The two lists from Adam to Noah and from Shem to Abram give each father's age when the next son was born, so they can be added up. The Hebrew (Masoretic) numbers give 1,656 years from creation to the flood, the Samaritan Pentateuch 1,307, and the Septuagint 2,242. After the flood the Hebrew gives 292 years to Abram's birth, the Samaritan 942 and the Septuagint, which adds a Cainan, 1,072. The variants at 5:3 and 11:12 give the numbers. Whether the lists are complete, and what the long ages mean, is discussed in the notes at 5:1 and 5:5.

Genesis is divided by the formula "this is the family history (toledot) of...": the heavens and earth (2:4), Adam (5:1), Noah (6:9), Noah's sons (10:1), Shem (11:10) and Terah (11:27) in chapters 1–11, then Ishmael, Isaac, Esau and Jacob. Each heading introduces what came from the person named.
sections.refs: Genesis 2:4; Genesis 5:1; Genesis 6:9; Genesis 10:1; Genesis 11:10; Genesis 11:27

common: The Bible says the world is exactly 6,000 years old.
uncommon: The Greek Bible's numbers put creation more than 5,000 years before Christ, and many early Christians used them.

sections.b: Two men named Enoch appear: Cain's son, after whom the first city is named (4:17), and the seventh from Adam in Seth's line (5:18–24). The second lives 365 years, "walked with God," and "was gone, for God took him." The Babylonian seventh king before the flood, Enmeduranki, was also said to be taken into the gods' presence (see the note at 5:23).

Genesis 6:4 places the Nephilim "on the earth in those days, and also afterward," alongside the unions of 6:2; it does not quite say the Nephilim were their children. The Greek translated Nephilim as "giants." The same word returns only in Numbers 13:33, where it expresses the spies' fear. The "heroes of long ago" (gibborim) link to Nimrod, "the first to become a hero on the earth" (10:8).

sections.h: Genesis 6–9: the shape of the story
sections.b: Gordon Wenham showed that the flood account is built as a mirror centered on "God remembered Noah" (8:1): seven days of waiting, forty days of rain, 150 days of rising waters, then 150 days of falling, forty days, and seven-day waits for the birds. The flood undoes creation (7:11 reverses 1:6–9) and the world is made again: wind over the waters, dry land, the blessing "be fruitful," and food (8:1–9:3). The story ends in a covenant with every living creature (9:8–17).

The Sumerian story of Ziusudra, the Babylonian Atrahasis, and Tablet XI of Gilgamesh all tell of a flood sent by the gods, a hero warned in advance, a boat, animals, birds sent out, and a sacrifice. Genesis shares this outline. It differs in having one God who judges violence, rather than gods annoyed by noise; a righteous man chosen by favor; and a covenant promise at the end.

common: The Bible says it had never rained before the flood.
uncommon: Some regional-flood readers hold that the flood covered only the inhabited world of Mesopotamia.

sections.b: Noah's father names him for "relief" from the cursed ground (5:29). He finds favor (6:8), is "righteous... blameless in his generations" and "walked with God" (6:9), and never speaks until he curses Canaan (9:25). He obeys every command (6:22; 7:5), builds the first altar (8:20), receives God's covenant (9:8–17), plants a vineyard and gets drunk (9:20–21). He lives 950 years.

The first covenant in the Bible is promised before the flood (6:18) and set out after it (9:8–17). It is made with Noah, all his descendants, every living creature and the earth itself. God binds himself never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets his bow in the clouds as the sign. The word "covenant" occurs seven times in 9:9–17. Before it come commands for all humanity: be fruitful, eat no blood, and answer for human life (9:1–7), the basis of the rabbinic laws of Noah.

Cain and Abel each bring a minchah, a gift, from their own work; God favors Abel's (4:3–5), and readers debate why (see the note at 4:4). After the flood Noah builds the first altar and offers whole burnt offerings of every clean animal and bird; the LORD smells the "soothing smell" and promises never again to curse the ground (8:20–21). Some Christians also see a hint of sacrifice in the garments of skin (3:21).

God creates humans "male and female" and blesses them to be fruitful (1:27–28). In the garden, the man alone is "not good" (2:18); the woman is made as his match, he greets her with a poem, and the narrator draws the lesson: a man leaves his parents, sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh (2:24). Sin brings struggle into the relationship (3:16). The first polygamist is Lamech, in Cain's violent line (4:19).

The first man in the Bible to take two wives is Lamech, seventh from Adam in Cain's line (4:19). The narrator makes no comment, but Lamech is also the man who boasts of killing (4:23–24). Genesis 2:24 had spoken of a man clinging to his wife, singular.

The story is a mirror: people speak one language, settle, say "Come, let's" twice, and build; at the center the LORD comes down to see; then he says "Come, let us," confuses the language, and scatters them, and the building stops. The puns pile up: bricks and mortar, Babel and balal (mix up). The builders fear being scattered and want a name; in the next chapter God promises Abram a great name (12:2). Chapter 10 has already shown the nations spread by language (10:5, 20, 31).

common: God punished people simply for building a tall building.
uncommon: Some Jewish interpreters read "one set of words" as one enforced ideology.

sections.b: Babylon enters the Bible as Babel, the first city of Nimrod's kingdom in Shinar (10:10), and the city of the tower (11:1–9). Genesis explains its name by balal, "confusion," mocking the Babylonians' own explanation, "gate of god." The great ziggurat of Babylon was called "House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth." Revelation's "Babylon the great" (Revelation 17–18) stands at the far end of this line.

Japheth's line runs north and west (Greeks, Medes, Anatolian peoples), Ham's south and southwest (Nubia, Egypt, Libya, Canaan, and Nimrod's Mesopotamian kingdom), Shem's east (Elam, Assyria, Aram, Arabia), and Shem's is placed last because it leads to Abram. Each section closes with "by their clans and their languages, in their lands and their nations" (10:5, 20, 31). Peleg's name marks a division (10:25).

Notes on this site that weigh specific parallels: the deep and Tiamat (1:2), sun and moon without names (1:16), sea monsters (1:21), humans from clay (2:7), the snake and the plant of life (2:9), the ten long-lived kings (5:3), the seventh king Enmeduranki (5:23), the size of the ark (6:15), the birds (8:8), the sacrifice (8:21), Marduk's bow (9:13), Nimrod (10:8), the spell of Nudimmud (11:1) and the ziggurat (11:4). Many scholars, conservative and critical, see Genesis as answering these traditions: one God, no battle, humans as royal images rather than slaves.
sections.refs: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 5:3; Genesis 8:8; Genesis 8:21; Genesis 11:4

claude.title: Genesis 1–11 read beside Atrahasis
claude.body: My own summary of a comparison first drawn by Kikawada and Quinn and by Frymer-Kensky: Atrahasis and Genesis 1–9 share the order creation of humans, trouble, flood, sacrifice and a settlement afterward. In Atrahasis the settlement is population control (barren women, infant death). In Genesis it is the opposite: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (9:1). If the writer knew a story like Atrahasis, the blessing of 9:1 may be a pointed reply.

sections.h: Elohim and YHWH Elohim in Genesis 1–4
sections.b: Genesis 1:1–2:3 uses only Elohim, "God," 35 times. Genesis 2:4–3:24 uses the double name YHWH Elohim, "the LORD God," 20 times, a combination rare elsewhere. The snake and the woman say only "God" (3:1–5). Eve uses YHWH at Cain's birth (4:1), and 4:26 says people "began to call on the LORD's name," a key text in the debate over Exodus 6:3 and the sources of the Torah.
sections.refs: Genesis 1:1; Genesis 2:4; Genesis 3:1–5; Genesis 4:1; Genesis 4:26; Exodus 6:3

sections.b: Genesis 1:2 has the ruach of God fluttering over the waters, a phrase that may mean God's Spirit or a mighty wind (see the note there). Christian readers have seen the Spirit at work in creation, with Psalm 104:30 ("You send your breath out, and they are created"), where "breath" is ruach, the word also used for the Spirit. God's "breath" also gives the man life (2:7), and in 6:3 God's spirit will not stay in humans forever.
Genesis 1 is the root of the Bible's teaching that God's word creates. Ten times "God said"; each time "and so it was." Psalm 33:6, 9, John 1:1–3 and Hebrews 11:3 build directly on it.
sections.refs: Genesis 1:3; Genesis 1:6; Genesis 1:9; Psalm 33:6–9; John 1:1–3; Hebrews 11:3

sections.b: The first cherubim in the Bible guard the way to the tree of life, east of Eden, with a flaming sword (Genesis 3:24). The same beings appear on the ark's cover, in the temple, in Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot, and, many scholars think, in Revelation's four living creatures.

Genesis 1–11 already tells a re-creation. The flood returns the world toward the watery deep of 1:2 (7:11), and then God sends a wind, makes dry land appear on New Year's Day, blesses humans to be fruitful, and gives them food again (8:1–9:3). The prophets and Revelation speak of a final new creation in the same terms: a new heaven and earth, no more curse, the tree of life (Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1; 22:2–3).
sections.refs: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:1–19; Genesis 9:1–3; Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1; Revelation 22:2–3

sections.h: The deep and the sea monsters in Genesis 1
sections.b: Genesis begins with darkness on "the deep" (tehom, 1:2). God divides the waters, gathers them into seas (1:9–10) and creates the great sea monsters as ordinary creatures (1:21). In the flood the deep breaks open again (7:11). Unlike the Babylonian epic, there is no battle: the sea is simply under God's command.

The first time the Bible uses chen, "favor" or "grace," is "Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes" (6:8), a pun on his name. Readers have long noted that this comes before Noah is called righteous (6:9).

sections.h: Magog in the Table of Nations
sections.b: Magog first appears as a son of Japheth, beside Meshech and Tubal (Genesis 10:2), peoples of the far north. Ezekiel 38–39 and Revelation 20:8 draw on these names.

Genesis 1–11 is preserved in the Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex, AD 1008, and the Aleppo Codex, which lacks most of the Torah), the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Greek Septuagint (200s BC), the Aramaic Targums, the Syriac and the Latin. Several small Dead Sea Scroll fragments from Qumran cover parts of chapters 1–6 (for example 4QGen-b, 4QGen-g, 4QGen-h, 4QGen-k and 6QpaleoGen); they mostly agree with the Masoretic Text, with spelling differences and a few readings such as "one gathering" in 1:9. The largest differences are the numbers in chapters 5 and 11, which produce three different chronologies, and the missing words of Cain in 4:8.

The first chapters of Genesis are where source criticism started. Jean Astruc (1753) noticed that Genesis 1:1–2:3 calls God only Elohim while 2:4–3:24 uses YHWH Elohim, and that the two creation accounts tell events in a different order (plants, animals, then male and female together in chapter 1; the man, the garden, the animals, then the woman in chapter 2). In the flood story the two names alternate, and so do pairs of details: two of every animal (6:19–20) or seven pairs of clean animals (7:2–3); forty days (7:12, 17) or 150 days (7:24); a dated calendar beside a count of weeks. Classic theory assigns 1:1–2:3, chapter 5, the flood dates and covenant (9:1–17) and 11:10–26 to P, and the garden, Cain, the vineyard and Babel to J. There is no E in Genesis 1–11 on almost any account.

sections.b: Readers who see one author or a single design answer each point. Cassuto argued that "God" names the Creator of all and "the LORD" the God who speaks with people, so the change of name follows the subject. Chapter 2 is often read as a close-up of the sixth day, not a second order of creation. Gordon Wenham found a large mirror pattern (chiasm) running through the whole flood story, with its center at 8:1, and argued that it fits a single account better than two woven together. Kikawada and Quinn compared Genesis 1–11 to the plan of Atrahasis (creation, a first crisis, a flood, a new start) and argued for the unity of the whole. Critical scholars reply that a final editor could produce such patterns from older sources. These are live debates, not settled questions.
